Family prefix: `LLM-AC-`.\\n\\nSeverity scale: CRITICAL > HIGH > MEDIUM > LOW > INFO. Thresholds without an AWS-published value are marked `workload-specific` at severity INFO.\\n\\n| check-id | pillar | severity | detection-rule | remediation | AWS-doc-citation |\\n|---|---|---|---|---|---|\\n| LLM-AC-001 | Security/Responsible-AI | CRITICAL | The AgentCore runtime execution role\\'s identity policies, evaluated statically (`iam:SimulatePrincipalPolicy` is never called; label \"evaluated from policy documents, not simulated\"), show a required action is denied \u2014 e.g. `bedrock:InvokeModel` / `bedrock:InvokeModelWithResponseStream`, `s3:GetObject` for artifacts/KB sources, `logs:CreateLogStream`/`logs:PutLogEvents`, or the `bedrock:` actions behind the `bedrock-agent-runtime` operations it calls (for example `bedrock:Retrieve`, `bedrock:InvokeAgent`). The agent cannot invoke models or read its dependencies. | Grant the runtime role least-privilege permissions for every action it exercises (model invoke on the specific model/inference-profile ARNs, S3 read on the source bucket, CloudWatch Logs write, gateway target actions); re-read the policies until every required action is allowed. | https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/runtime-permissions.html |\\n| LLM-AC-002 | Security/Responsible-AI | HIGH | An Organizations SCP applies an explicit `Deny` to actions AgentCore needs (`bedrock:*`, `bedrock-agentcore:*`, or specific invoke/gateway actions) for the account/OU, so an otherwise-correct runtime role is still blocked. Detect by reading effective SCPs (`organizations:ListPoliciesForTarget` / `DescribePolicy`) and correlating with the denied action from the policy read. | Amend the SCP (or move the account to an OU) so the required AgentCore actions are not explicitly denied; an explicit SCP deny overrides any identity-based allow. | https://docs.aws.amazon.com/organizations/latest/userguide/orgs_manage_policies_scps.html |\\n| LLM-AC-003 | Reliability | HIGH | `ec2:DescribeVpcEndpoints` shows an endpoint missing for a VPC-deployed runtime in subnets without internet access. AWS documents `com.amazonaws.<region>.ecr.dkr`, `com.amazonaws.<region>.ecr.api`, the S3 gateway endpoint `com.amazonaws.<region>.s3` and `com.amazonaws.<region>.logs` as required; the agent also needs an endpoint for each AWS service its own code calls (for example `bedrock-runtime` for model calls, `bedrock-agent-runtime` for knowledge base retrieval). Traffic with no private path fails in no-egress subnets. | Create the missing endpoints (interface endpoints for ECR, Logs and the services the code calls; the S3 gateway endpoint, which AWS recommends even with a NAT gateway) with security groups allowing HTTPS from the agent subnets; verify DNS resolution and a test invocation. | https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/agentcore-vpc.html |\\n| LLM-AC-004 | Reliability | HIGH | The AgentCore gateway is not configured, or a gateway target is misconfigured \u2014 no gateway associated with the agent, a target endpoint/credential/schema invalid, or the target health check failing. The most common cause is that the agent code never actually uses the memory. Here are the checks, most likely cause first.

**1. Does the agent code write and read events on every turn? (most common cause)**
- AgentCore Memory only holds what your code writes with `CreateEvent` and reads back with `ListEvents` or `GetEvent`. Creating a memory resource does not capture conversations on its own.
- A runtime `runtimeSessionId` only routes requests to a microVM. It stores no conversation history.
- Confirm that each invoke loads prior events before calling the model and writes the new user and assistant messages afterward.

**2. Are `memoryId`, `actorId` and `sessionId` the same across turns?**
- Short-term events are scoped by `memoryId` + `actorId` + `sessionId`. If any of the three changes between turns, the agent reads an empty history.
- A new `sessionId` per request is a common mistake. Use a stable ID per conversation.
- If you don't send an `actorId`, the starter templates fall back to `default`. Then every caller shares one history instead of getting their own.
- In multi-agent setups, agents only share context if they use the same memory resource and the same actor and session scoping.

**3. Are you expecting long-term memory to work like chat history?**
- Long-term records are extracted asynchronously by the memory strategies (semantic, summarization, user preference, episodic or custom). They can take a few minutes to appear, so they won't help the next turn.
- Check that the strategy namespaces and `extractionConfig` are valid. A bad namespace variable still stores the event but can silently skip extraction.
- Retrieval uses `RetrieveMemoryRecords` or `ListMemoryRecords` against those namespaces. If your namespace template uses `{actorId}` or `{sessionId}`, the retrieval call has to use the same values.
- Blob payloads are never extracted.
- Enable log delivery on the memory to see extraction errors.

**4. Are you using branches?**
- Events written to one branch after a fork don't appear in another, and there is no merge operation. If your code creates branches, make sure it reads from the branch it wrote to.

**5. Are Memory calls failing or being throttled?**
- `CreateEvent` is limited to 5 TPS per actor per session. Throttled writes mean later turns are missing from history.
- Check the Memory CloudWatch metrics (`Invocations`, `Latency` and `Errors` for `CreateEvent` and `ListEvents`) and the runtime logs for swallowed exceptions.
- Check the runtime execution role for `bedrock-agentcore` memory actions (`CreateEvent`, `ListEvents` and `RetrieveMemoryRecords`). An IAM or SCP deny there can fail quietly if the code catches the error.
- If the runtime or memory is in another account, the resource-based policy has to allow each Memory action separately.

**6. Check the stored data directly.** The AgentCore CLI lets you see what is actually in the memory:
```
agentcore memory actor list --id <memory-id>
agentcore memory session list --id <memory-id> --actor-id <actor-id>
agentcore memory event list --id <memory-id> --actor-id <actor-id> --session-id <session-id>
agentcore memory record list --id <memory-id> --namespace-path /
```
Compare the results with the IDs your agent sends:
- **No events at all:** the agent isn't writing (check 1) or the write is failing (check 5).
- **Events under unexpected actors or sessions:** the IDs are inconsistent (check 2).
- **Events present but the agent still forgets:** the read path or prompt assembly is the problem, not storage.
